claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is in a BCC state at high temperature.
Annealing Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 at or above 1400 °C ensures complete homogenization and establishes a uniform BCC state.
Configurational entropy stabilizes the BCC phase of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 at high temperature.
Strong Al-induced ordering creates a thermodynamic instability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 as temperature decreases.
Al-Co, Al-Fe, and Al-Ni interactions have large negative mixing enthalpies and therefore strong ordering tendencies.
The ordering instability becomes manifest only when atomic diffusion is sufficiently active.
Lowering temperature reduces entropic stabilization and exposes the thermodynamic driving force for ordering.
Slow cooling with dwell times through 1350–1100 °C permits diffusional ordering in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Longer residence time in critical thermal intervals can alter phase nucleation, phase fraction, and grain growth in multicomponent alloys.
Cooling rate can control phase selection in high-entropy alloys through kinetic effects.
Al-induced short-range-order clusters act as precursors to nucleation and growth of a more stable ordered phase.
Diffusion during slow cooling allows ordered clusters to form and grow, ultimately destabilizing the BCC phase.
Rapid quenching limits diffusion and suppresses ordering.
Rapid quenching preserves a metastable BCC state in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Slow-cooled samples will show greater atomic ordering, including superlattice reflections and ordered domains, than rapidly quenched samples.
Rapidly quenched samples will largely retain the high-temperature BCC structure without significant ordering.
The controlled comparison uses identically homogenized samples subjected either to slow cooling with dwells or to rapid quenching under the same inert atmosphere.
Failure of slow cooling to produce a statistically significant increase in ordering relative to quenching would falsify the proposed kinetic-ordering mechanism.

contradictions.description: The baseline says observed differences would be solely due to cooling-rate variation, but the slow-cooled group also receives extended dwell times while the quenched group does not. Cooling rate and residence time are therefore changed together.
